newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Aid groups meet to coordinate stance over Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Aid groups meet to coordinate stance over Taleban.

text.p: Western aid groups in Kabul, concerned about the ban on women working imposed by the new Taleban rulers, say they plan to make a joint approach to the fundamentalist militia.

In the week since they took over the capital, the Taleban have moved to exert control over the country and impose their purist brand of fundamentalist Islam on the capital, ordering women to stay at home and forcing men to worship.

Aid officials said it may be impossible to operate according to their organisations' mandates or attract governmental assistance so long as the Taleban bar women from working or hinder them from receiving help.
They said its attitude threatens key aid programmes in one of the world's poorest countries.

Aid workers from U.N. projects and about 15 NGOs said they would meet later on Saturday to finalise a unified approach to the Taleban administration, hoping to present the Shura, or ruling council, with a joint statement.

The Taleban say they will work out a way for women to work separately from men, but have given no time frame. Since the current ban has been in force, aid groups have told their women workers to stay at home.
"We could send a car for them, but the entire neighbourhood would know. It is too dangerous," said one aid official.
The Taleban captured Kabul late last month after a lightning offensive, surprising the local population with the speed of the takeover.
Since then it has issued decrees restricting women's activities and ordering men to grow beards and attend prayers five times a day.
The capital has been largely peaceful since the takeover, although armed Taleban guards have been seen beating women who venture out of doors without wearing the all-embracing Islamic veil.
On Friday, guards pulled men from their vehicles into the city's main mosque to pray.

Aid officials said their main problem was conforming with mandates that bar sexual discrimination but they also said it would be hard to persuade Western governments to provide funding under the present conditions.
In addition, the practicalities of separating women and men in the workplace and in programmes could make operations impossible, the said.
"I think we all agree that we should do the winter programme at any cost because there is a highly vulnerable population facing severe weather with few resources," said one.
Groups operating in Kabul include the International Committee of the Red Cross, which distributes food, and some non-governmental organisations (NGOs) conducting medical projects.

At least 200,000 people in Kabul receive daily help, mainly food from Western-sponsored programmes. Many hospitals and clinics get supplies, salaries and doctors from Western agencies that are also involved in providing water and sanitation to Kabul and other areas.

Most Western aid projects have ground to a halt since the takeover, in part because women were not turning up for medical treatment. Some aid officials said they did not want to confront the Taleban and were hopeful after some members of the shura expressed understanding of aid groups' attitude.
Such groups are often dependent on Afghan women, especially those whose projects are designed to help women and children.
Taleban leaders had assured aid groups that the situation would improve once most of its fighters had been moved out of the city, but had given no timeframe.
